title: Certified Diagnosis Sets with an Out-of-Envelope Alarm for Hydraulic Condition Monitoring: Evidence from a Public Test-Rig Data Set
abstract: Condition monitoring of hydraulic equipment usually returns a single fault label, even when the data resemble nothing seen during training. This study evaluates a diagnosis that returns a set of possible condition grades with a stated confidence and treats an empty set as an out-of-envelope alarm. We use the public UCI data set of a hydraulic test rig (2205 load cycles, 17 sensors, four components: cooler, valve, pump leakage and accumulator), summarise each cycle by six statistics per sensor, and apply a random forest with split-conformal calibration at the 95% level. With random splits of cycles, five-fold accuracy was 0.985 to 0.998 and set coverage was 0.948 to 0.969, with a mean set size below one. When calibration used stable cycles and testing used the 756 cycles flagged as not yet stable, coverage fell to between 0.21 and 0.60, so the guarantee did not survive this shift. However, the share of empty sets rose from 3%–5% to 11%–73%, which makes the empty set usable as an alarm. All results come from one test rig and no field data were used; the method is a diagnostic aid, not a safety function.

Abstract

Condition monitoring of hydraulic equipment usually returns a single fault label, even when the data resemble nothing seen during training. This study evaluates a diagnosis that returns a set of possible condition grades with a stated confidence and treats an empty set as an out-of-envelope alarm. We use the public UCI data set of a hydraulic test rig (2205 load cycles, 17 sensors, four components: cooler, valve, pump leakage and accumulator), summarise each cycle by six statistics per sensor, and apply a random forest with split-conformal calibration at the 95% level. With random splits of cycles, five-fold accuracy was 0.985 to 0.998 and set coverage was 0.948 to 0.969, with a mean set size below one. When calibration used stable cycles and testing used the 756 cycles flagged as not yet stable, coverage fell to between 0.21 and 0.60, so the guarantee did not survive this shift. However, the share of empty sets rose from 3%–5% to 11%–73%, which makes the empty set usable as an alarm. All results come from one test rig and no field data were used; the method is a diagnostic aid, not a safety function.
Keywords: hydraulic systems; condition monitoring; fault diagnosis; conformal prediction; uncertainty quantification; distribution shift
1. Introduction

Hydraulic systems drive the actuators of offshore platforms, process plants and mobile machinery, and their components degrade gradually: a cooler loses efficiency, a valve switches more slowly, a pump leaks internally and an accumulator loses its pre-charge pressure. Condition-monitoring software classifies the grade of each component from the sensor signals of the working cycle (Helwig et al., 2015). Most classifiers return one label. A planner who receives a label has no way to tell whether the label is certain or a guess, and no warning when the machine runs in conditions that the classifier has never seen.

Conformal prediction replaces the single label by a set of labels that contains the true one with a stated probability, under the assumption that calibration and test data are exchangeable (Vovk et al., 2005; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021). A set with one label is a confident diagnosis, a set with several labels is an ambiguous one, and an empty set says that no grade is consistent with the data at the stated level. The empty set is therefore a natural out-of-envelope alarm. The question of this paper is whether, on a real test rig, these sets reach their stated coverage when cycles come from the same conditions, what happens to coverage when the operating conditions change, and whether the empty set is then a useful alarm.

The paper contributes (i) an evaluation of conformal diagnosis sets for four hydraulic components on a public data set, (ii) an explicit test under a shift from stable to not-yet-stable operating cycles, and (iii) the finding that the coverage guarantee fails under this shift while the empty-set rate rises sharply.
2. Related work

The data set used here was released with a study of condition monitoring of a hydraulic rig by multivariate statistics (Helwig et al., 2015). Random forests are a standard classifier for such tabular features (Breiman, 2001). Split-conformal prediction calibrates a threshold on held-out cycles (Vovk et al., 2005), and for classification the least ambiguous set rule of Sadinle et al. (2019), which keeps every class whose probability is high enough, gives the smallest sets for a given coverage; this is the score used here. Adaptive and cost-aware set constructions exist (Romano et al., 2020).

Predictive uncertainty is known to degrade under dataset shift (Ovadia et al., 2019), and conformal methods for covariate shift reweight the calibration data (Tibshirani et al., 2019). We do not apply such corrections: we ask what a plain split-conformal set does under a shift, because that is what a maintenance team would deploy first. Our searches did not find a published conformal analysis of this hydraulic data set; the search was not exhaustive.
3. Data

We use the UCI data set Condition monitoring of hydraulic systems (ZeMA gGmbH; Helwig et al., 2015; licence CC BY 4.0). A test rig repeats a load cycle of 60 seconds 2205 times while the condition of four components is varied. Each cycle is recorded by 17 sensors (six pressure sensors, motor power, two flow sensors, four temperature sensors, a vibration sensor and three derived values for cooling efficiency, cooling power and system efficiency), sampled at rates between 1 and 100 Hz. For each cycle the data set gives the condition grade of each component: cooler efficiency at 3, 20 or 100%, valve switching behaviour at 73, 80, 90 or 100%, pump leakage at grade 0, 1 or 2, and accumulator pressure at 90, 100, 115 or 130 bar. A further flag marks the cycles whose operating conditions had not yet stabilised: 1449 cycles are stable and 756 are not.
The data are public and contain no personal information. They were used as supplied.
4. Method
Features. Each sensor series of a cycle is summarised by six statistics: mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum and the 10th and 90th percentile, which gives 102 features per cycle.
Classifier. A random forest with 200 trees is trained separately for each component. Point accuracy and macro-averaged F1 are computed by stratified five-fold cross-validation.

Conformal sets. For random-split evaluation, the cycles are split 60/20/20 into training, calibration and test parts, 20 times with different seeds. The calibration score of a cycle is one minus the predicted probability of its true grade; the threshold is the ceil((n + 1) x (1 - alpha))-th smallest score, with alpha = 0.05. A grade belongs to the set of a test cycle if one minus its predicted probability does not exceed the threshold (Sadinle et al., 2019). We report coverage, mean set size, the share of empty sets and the lowest per-class coverage, as means and standard deviations over the 20 splits.
Shift. For the stable-to-unstable test, 70% of the stable cycles train the forest, the remaining 30% calibrate the threshold, and all 756 cycles flagged as not yet stable form the test part.
5. Results

With random splits of cycles, the forest classified the components almost perfectly (Table 1): five-fold accuracy was 0.998 for the cooler, 0.985 for the valve, 0.997 for pump leakage and 0.990 for the accumulator. Conformal coverage at the 95% level was between 0.948 and 0.969, close to the target, and the mean set size was below one for all components, which means that empty sets were more frequent than sets with several grades: 3% to 5% of the test cycles.
Table 1. Random-split results at the 95% level (60/20/20 splits repeated 20 times; accuracy and F1 by stratified five-fold cross-validation).

Under the stable-to-unstable shift the guarantee failed (Table 2). Coverage fell to 0.599 for the cooler, 0.205 for the valve, 0.269 for pump leakage and 0.519 for the accumulator. The share of empty sets rose to 40%, 53%, 73% and 11%. The point accuracy under the shift differed strongly between components (1.000 for pump leakage, 0.426 for the valve).
Table 2. Results when calibration used stable cycles and the test part was the 756 cycles flagged as not yet stable (95% level).

For pump leakage the point accuracy under the shift was 1.000 although coverage was only 0.269: the classifier was right, but its probabilities were lower than in calibration, so the threshold removed the true grade from the set. The empty set therefore signals a change in the data and not necessarily a wrong diagnosis.
6. Discussion and limitations

The sets reached their stated coverage when cycles came from the same distribution, and they did not when the operating conditions changed. This is what the theory predicts, but it matters for use: a maintenance team that reads a 95% set as a promise will be wrong on the cycles on which the rig is not yet in a stable state. What the shift did produce is a strong increase of empty sets, from 3–5% to 11–73%, so the empty set marks, in this data, the cycles on which the confidence statement cannot be trusted. We suggest that a work-order rule uses the output in three steps: a single grade goes to planning, a set with several grades to inspection, and an empty set to a check of the operating state before any decision. The rule was not tested with an operator.

Limits of the study. All data come from one test rig, and the grades are set by the experimenters and not produced by wear in service. The random splits put cycles of the same rig and of neighbouring conditions into training and test parts, so the near-perfect accuracy is an upper bound for a rig that has been seen before and says little about a new asset. The shift we tested is one defined by the data set's own stability flag; other shifts, such as a new rig or a sensor drift, were not examined. The calibration needs labelled cycles of each asset, so it has to be repeated on every new machine. The empty-set rate depends on the threshold and was not tuned as an alarm: we report no false-alarm rate against a ground truth of out-of-envelope states. No field data from an operating platform were used, and nothing here is a safety function.
7. Conclusion

On a public hydraulic test-rig data set, conformal diagnosis sets for four components had a coverage of 0.948 to 0.969 at the 95% level on random splits and only 0.21 to 0.60 when the calibration used stable cycles and the test used cycles that were not yet stable. The share of empty sets rose from 3%–5% to 11%–73% in the same shift, so the empty set is usable as an out-of-envelope alarm even though the coverage guarantee is lost. Confirming this for operating equipment needs data from several assets and an operator study.
Implementation and reproducibility

The study is implemented in the repository articles-hydroguard-fdd: features.py (cycle statistics), conformal.py (threshold, sets and evaluation), data.py (download and loading of the public data) and scripts/run_experiment.py, which writes every number in Tables 1 and 2 to outputs/results.json; one unit test on synthetic data checks the coverage of the conformal sets and is not used for any reported result. The numbers in this paper are those stored in outputs/results.json, produced by the author's run of the script on the public data.
Data and code availability

The data set is public (UCI Machine Learning Repository, CC BY 4.0) and is downloaded by the script, not stored in the repository. The analysis code and result files are in the author's private repository and are available on request.
